notes.40:26: The second-person singular pronoun σε ("your notice") in the closing clause is debated as addressing either Israel (anticipating Jacob in v. 27) or God in an abrupt apostrophe, differing from the Hebrew "not one is missing."
notes.40:29: Where the Hebrew text speaks of increasing power for the weak, the Greek text reads "sorrow to those who are not suffering pain," reflecting a different reading of the underlying Hebrew root for strength/trouble.
notes.41:1: The Greek reads "Renew yourselves" (Ἐγκαινίζεσθε) and "rulers" (ἄρχοντες), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("Keep silence" and "peoples").
notes.41:2: In Greek, "righteousness" (δικαιοσύνην) is feminine (referred to by feminine "it" here and in v. 4), leaving "Who" (God, v. 4) as the grammatical antecedent for the masculine pronouns and verbs in vv. 2-3.
notes.41:7: Following "and he will say" at the end of v. 6, the Greek introduces the craftsman's words directly at the start of v. 7, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Be strong!" in v. 6 and begins narrative action in v. 7.
notes.41:14: The Greek reads "tiny Israel" (ὀλιγοστὸς Ἰσραήλ, smallest or fewest in number) rather than "you worm Jacob / men of Israel" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.41:16: The Greek has plural "the holy ones of Israel" (τοῖς ἁγίοις Ἰσραήλ), contrasting with the singular "the Holy One of Israel" in v. 20 and in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.42:1: The Septuagint explicitly identifies the servant and chosen one as "Jacob" and "Israel," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text leaves them unnamed; accordingly, third-person pronouns in vv. 1-4 refer to Jacob/Israel.
notes.42:6: The Greek source text ends v. 6 at "a covenant of a race" (εἰς διαθήκην γένους) without the phrase "a light to the nations" found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and some Greek manuscripts.
notes.42:10: The phrase ἡ ἀρχὴ αὐτοῦ literally means "its beginning" (referring to the new hymn) or "His dominion," where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "His praise."
notes.42:19: The Greek differs substantially from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, speaking of "My servants" (plural), "those who rule over them" (rather than "My messenger"), and "the servants of God were blinded."
notes.42:24: The Greek text begins with the dative relative pronoun οἷς ("upon those to whom"), connecting syntactically with "the things to come" in v. 23, whereas other Greek manuscripts and the Hebrew Masoretic Text read "Who gave...?"
notes.43:3: The Greek text reads "Syene" (ancient Aswan in Upper Egypt) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Seba."
notes.43:6: Greek "to the southwest" (from Greek lips, the southwest wind or quarter) stands here where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "to the south."
notes.43:12: Greek "I reproached" and "among us" (following the first-person plural pronoun in the Greek critical text) differ from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "I proclaimed" and "among you."
notes.43:15: The Greek participial construction ("who appointed Israel as your king") places "Israel" and "your king" in the accusative as object and complement, differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("Creator of Israel, your King").
notes.43:20: The Greek text renders the desert creatures literally as "sirens and daughters of ostriches," traditional Septuagint designations for Hebrew "jackals and ostriches."
notes.44:2: Greek "beloved Israel" translates the Hebrew poetic name "Jeshurun," and the Greek places "You will yet be helped" at the start of the direct address.
notes.44:5: Greek epigrapsei cheiri autou uses the compound verb epigraphein ("inscribe upon") with a bare dative, which can denote either the instrument ("write with his hand") or the surface inscribed ("inscribe on his hand").
notes.44:6: Greek "God Sabaoth" leaves Hebrew "Sabaoth" (hosts/armies) transliterated rather than translated, and reads "after these things" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "the last."
notes.44:11: Greek "deaf ones from among people" likely arose from reading Hebrew harashim ("craftsmen") as hereshim ("deaf ones"), and "all from whom they came have dried up" differs from the Hebrew "all his associates will be put to shame."
notes.44:26: The Greek text reads "the cities of Idumea" (Edom) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the cities of Judah."
notes.44:28: Greek "tells Cyrus to be wise" (phronein) differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "says of Cyrus, 'He is My shepherd,'" and Greek "I will lay the foundation" is first-person active rather than passive.
notes.45:4: In the Greek Septuagint, God tells Cyrus "I will call you by My name" (τῷ ὀνόματί μου) and "accept you," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("call you by your name" and "give you a title of honor").
notes.45:7: The plural κακά ("evils") is set in contrast with "peace" (εἰρήνην); in such a pairing it can denote calamities or adversity.
notes.45:9: The Greek opens with the distinct Septuagint reading "What better thing have I fashioned like potter's clay?" and includes the plowman question (cf. Isaiah 28:24) as well as the closing question echoed in Romans 9:20.
notes.45:14: "Sabaoth" (σαβαώθ) is the Septuagint transliteration of Hebrew tseva'ot ("of hosts/armies"), and "Ethiopians" (Αἰθιόπων) renders Hebrew Cush. In the nations' prayer, "besides You" shifts from addressing Zion ("in you") to addressing God directly (continued in 45:15).
notes.45:23: The clause "εἰ μὴ ἐξελεύσεται..." reflects the Septuagint's Hebraistic oath formula after "I swear" (ὀμνύω), expressing positive certainty ("that... will surely go out"); the Greek also explicitly specifies "by God" (τὸν θεόν) at the end of the verse.
notes.46:1: The Greek phrase ἐγένετο ... εἰς ("have come to be for") reflects the Hebrew idiom meaning they became burdens placed upon wild beasts and livestock.
notes.46:4: The repeated ἐγώ εἰμι ("I am") echoes the absolute divine self-designation in 45:18-19; ἀνήσω ("I will forgive/spare/release") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("I will carry/bear").
notes.46:10: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "things that have not yet been done," the Greek reads καὶ ἅμα συνετελέσθη ("and at once it was accomplished").
notes.46:12: "You who have lost heart" translates the distinct Septuagint reading οἱ ἀπολωλεκότες τὴν καρδίαν, differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("stout/stubborn of heart").
notes.47:2: "Your gray hairs" (τὰς πολιάς) is a distinct Septuagint reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "the skirt/train."
notes.47:3: The verb παραδῶ ("yield" or "hand over") appears without an expressed direct object in the Greek (differing from the Hebrew "I will not spare any man"), and 47:4 shifts to singular "rescues you" (σε) against the Hebrew plural "our Redeemer."
notes.47:9: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("these two things... in one day, loss of children and widowhood"), the Greek omits the explicit subject and leaves ἥξει ("it will come") with an implied subject carried over from 47:8.
notes.47:14: The Greek reverses the sense of the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("there is no coal for warming, no fire to sit before"), reading instead an ironic command: "for you have coals of fire—sit upon them!"
notes.48:2: "Sabaoth" transliterates the Septuagint's indeclinable Greek sabaōth (from Hebrew "hosts/armies"), which Greek Isaiah frequently retains untranslated rather than rendering it as "hosts" or "Almighty."
notes.48:6: In vv. 6-7 the Septuagint reads "and you did not say, 'Now it is happening...'" rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "hidden things you did not know. Now they are created."
notes.48:9: The Septuagint differs markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text here, reading "I will show you My wrath, and I will bring My glorious deeds upon you" instead of deferring anger, and similarly in v. 10 reading "I have sold you" and "furnace of poverty" rather than refining in affliction.
notes.48:14: In contrast to the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("the Lord loves him; he shall perform His purpose on Babylon, and His arm against the Chaldeans"), the Septuagint renders the clause in the first person addressed to Israel: "Loving you, I carried out your will against Babylon, to remove the seed of the Chaldeans."
notes.48:16: The doubled divine title translates Greek kyrios Kyrios, the Septuagint rendering of Hebrew Adonai YHWH (also in 50:5, 7). Commentators debate whether the same divine speaker continues ("sent Me") or whether the prophet or Servant begins speaking at "and now."
notes.49:1: The Septuagint translates Hebrew "from afar" temporally as "after a long time" and supplies "it will stand, says the Lord."
notes.49:5: Greek syntax shifts abruptly after "and Israel" into the Servant's parenthetical declaration ("I will be gathered and glorified..."), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("though Israel be not gathered").
notes.49:6: The Septuagint reads "It is a great thing for you" (against Hebrew "It is too small a thing") and includes "as a covenant for a people" before "as a light for nations."
notes.49:7: The Septuagint opens the divine speech with the imperative "Sanctify" (against Hebrew "to the despised of soul") and renders "servant of rulers" as plural "servants of the rulers" in apposition to "the nations."
notes.49:12: The Septuagint identifies the distant region as "the land of the Persians" (corresponding to "Sinim" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text), and "the sea" reflects the Hebrew directional idiom for the west.
notes.50:1: Greek hypochreō literally means "debtor" (here translating the Hebrew word for "creditor"), and Poion asks "What is" rather than Hebrew "Where is."
notes.50:4: Instead of the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "how to sustain the weary with a word," the Septuagint reads "to know when one ought to speak a word," and pairs "He set" (ethēken) with "He added" (prosethēken) where Hebrew repeats "He awakens."
notes.50:5: The Septuagint specifies "the instruction (paidia) of the Lord, the Lord, opens my ears," explicitly linking this verse with the "tongue of instruction" in v. 4.
notes.50:11: Following the Septuagint, v. 11 reads "strengthen a flame" (for Hebrew "gird yourselves with firebrands"), casts "these things happened to you" in the past tense, and ends with "in sorrow" (lypē) rather than "in torment."
notes.51:3: The Greek renders the Hebrew region name ("her Arabah") as "the regions toward the west" (τὰ πρὸς δυσμάς) and uses παράδεισος ("paradise") for both Hebrew "Eden" and "garden."
notes.51:9: Unlike the Hebrew text, which addresses the arm of the Lord, the Greek explicitly addresses Jerusalem (Ἰερουσαλήμ), which also governs the feminine participles in 51:10.
notes.51:15: The title Κύριος σαβαώθ ("the Lord Sabaoth") leaves the Hebrew title ṣəbāʾôt ("hosts" or "armies") transliterated in Greek; the same title recurs in 54:5.
notes.51:16: Because Σειών ("Zion") is indeclinable, it functions here as a bare dative "to Zion" (as in 52:7, λέγων Σειών), though grammatically it could also be construed as the subject ("and Zion will say").
notes.51:20: The Greek uniquely renders the Hebrew simile ("like an antelope in a net") as ὡς σευτλίον ἡμίεφθον ("like a half-boiled beet").
notes.52:4: The doubled title κύριος Κύριος ("the Lord, the Lord") translates Hebrew ʾădōnāy YHWH, and βίᾳ ἤχθησαν ("they were led by force") diverges from the Hebrew clause about oppression without cause.
notes.52:6: Greek ὡς ὥρα ("like a season") denotes a timely season, springtime, or bloom/beauty, corresponding to the Hebrew exclamation "How lovely" at the beginning of 52:7.
notes.52:14: Unlike the Hebrew text, which shifts to the third person in the second half of the verse, the Greek retains second-person singular pronouns (σέ, σου) throughout and uses Hebraic comparative ἀπό ("from" or "beyond").
notes.52:15: Greek θαυμάσονται ("will marvel") corresponds to Hebrew yazzeh ("he will sprinkle"), continuing the motif of astonishment from 52:14.
notes.53:1: ἀκοή means "what is heard," that is, a report or message. The verbs are aorists. The Greek adds the address "Lord" at the start, as quoted in John 12:38 and Romans 10:16.
notes.53:2: ἀνηγγείλαμεν means "we announced"; this is the Greek's own reading and differs from the Hebrew "he grew up." "Before him" may refer to the Lord.
notes.53:3: πληγή (a blow, stroke or plague) is rendered "plague" throughout the chapter (53:3, 4, 10), so that "cleanse him from the plague" in 53:10 keeps the link. λογίζομαι is rendered "reckon" in 53:3, 4 and 12.
notes.53:4: The Greek reads "bears our sins," not "griefs," and its verbs are present tense, kept here.
notes.53:5: παιδεία means "discipline, correction, instruction." μώλωψ is a welt or bruise left by a blow; the singular "bruise" follows the Greek.
notes.53:8: This is the Greek form quoted in Acts 8:32–33. ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνομιῶν can mean "because of" or "from" the lawless deeds; "because of" fits the context.
notes.53:9: In the Greek the Lord speaks in the first person, "I will give the wicked in exchange for his burial." This differs from the Hebrew and is rendered as it stands.
notes.53:10: The Saints Greek Critical Text reads ἡμῶν ("our soul"); many editions read ὑμῶν ("your soul"). The rendering follows the Saints text. περὶ ἁμαρτίας is the standard Septuagint expression for a sin offering.
notes.53:11: The Greek infinitives are kept in sequence ("to take away... to show... to form... to justify"). πλάσαι τῇ συνέσει, "to form (him) with understanding," is the Greek's own wording.
notes.53:12: ἀνθ᾽ ὧν means "in return for which," that is, "because." παραδίδωμι is rendered "hand over" in 53:6 and 53:12.
notes.54:9: The Greek reads "From the water in the time of Noah" (ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕδατος) rather than "Like the waters of Noah," and inserts the dative τῇ γῇ ("to the earth") before the oath about the mountains (54:9-10).
notes.54:10: The Greek closes with εἶπεν γάρ Ἵλεώς σοι, Κύριε ("for he said, 'Merciful to you, Lord'"), with vocative Κύριε (contrast nominative Κύριος in some witnesses) rendering Hebrew "says the Lord who has compassion on you."
notes.54:15: Greek προσήλυτοι προσελεύσονταί ("proselytes will come") introduces a wordplay on proselytes joining Zion through God (δι᾽ ἐμοῦ), differing substantially from the Hebrew warning against attackers.
notes.54:16: The Greek makes Zion itself the object of ἔκτισά σε ("I created you") rather than the smith, and negates the closing purpose clause ("not for destruction, to ruin").
notes.54:17: In "those guilty against you will be in it" (οἱ δὲ ἔνοχοί σου ἔσονται ἐν αὐτῇ), the feminine pronoun αὐτῇ ("it") refers back to κρίσιν ("judgment").
notes.55:1: The Greek has genitive οἴνου ("of wine") alongside accusative στέαρ ("fat," reading the Hebrew consonants ḥlb as "fat" rather than "milk").
notes.55:3: The phrase τὰ ὅσια Δαυὶδ τὰ πιστά (literally "the faithful holy things of David") translates Hebrew "faithful mercies of David" and is quoted in this Septuagint form in Acts 13:34.
notes.55:11: The Septuagint reads "and I will prosper your ways and My commands," differing from the Masoretic Text ("and it will succeed in the thing for which I sent it").
notes.55:13: Greek στοιβή (thorny burnet/thornbush) and κόνυζα (fleabane) identify specific Mediterranean plants, and "the Lord" (Κύριος) is the grammatical subject of "will be" rather than "for the Lord" as in Hebrew.
notes.56:6: The Greek specifies both genders ("male and female servants," δούλους καὶ δούλας) and shifts from the dative ("as for the foreigners") to the accusative ("and all who keep...") anticipating "I will bring them" in v. 7.
notes.56:8: The Septuagint uses the cognate noun συναγωγήν ("a gathering") and singular "him" (αὐτόν, referring to Israel).
notes.56:10: Greek ἴδετε ("See") reads the Hebrew consonants as an imperative rather than "his watchmen," and treats κοίτην ("bed") as the object or scene of their dreaming.
notes.56:11: Greek πονηροί ("wicked") reflects reading the Hebrew consonants rʿym as "evil" rather than "shepherds."
notes.57:2: The Septuagint explicitly mentions "his burial" (ἡ ταφὴ αὐτοῦ) and repeats the verb ἦρται ("has been taken away") from v. 1.
notes.57:5: Greek παρακαλοῦντες τὰ εἴδωλα ("entreat/comfort the idols") reflects reading the Hebrew verb from nḥm ("comfort/appeal to") rather than ḥmm ("be inflamed with lust").
notes.57:8: The clause "you thought that if you turned away from Me, you would have something more" is a distinctive Septuagint rendering diverging from the Masoretic Text.
notes.57:15: The phrase ἐν ἁγίοις can mean either "in the holy places" (parallel to ἐν ὑψηλοῖς, "in the high places") or "among the holy ones"; "giving patience to the fainthearted" also differs from Hebrew "to revive the spirit of the lowly."
notes.57:21: The Septuagint reads χαίρειν ("rejoicing") instead of Hebrew "peace," and ὁ θεός ("God") rather than "my God."
notes.58:4: LXX reads "strike a humble person with fists" (tapeinon) and "in an outcry" (en krauge), where the Hebrew MT has "with a wicked fist" and "on high."
notes.58:6: LXX uses ouchi ... alla ("I did not choose such a fast ... rather, loose...") as a negative contrast with v. 5, whereas MT frames v. 6 as an affirmative rhetorical question ("Is not this the fast that I choose...?").
notes.58:9: Greek cheirotonia (normally "stretching out the hand to vote/appoint") here renders Hebrew "pointing the finger" as an accusatory gesture, and "a word of grumbling" (rhema gongysmou) corresponds to MT "speaking wickedness."
notes.58:12: LXX "you will cause your paths in the midst to cease" renders the Hebrew infinitive lasebet ("to dwell") as if derived from sbt ("to cease").
notes.58:13: Greek shifts after "If you turn" (subjunctive) to future indicatives ("will call ... will not lift ... nor speak") and specifies "for work" and "in anger," which are absent from MT.
notes.59:5: Greek ourion specifically denotes a "wind-egg" (an unfertilized or addled egg), differing from MT "that which is crushed."
notes.59:11: LXX keeps the third-person plural ("they will go together") from vv. 9-10 before shifting to first-person plural ("we waited"), and turns MT's "we all growl like bears and moan like doves" into walking together.
notes.59:16: Greek emynato autous means "He defended them" (as in Acts 7:24, matching Heb. "saved"), though in Greek it can also mean "retaliated against them"; "with mercy" (te eleemosyne) renders MT "His righteousness."
notes.59:18: LXX joins v. 18 directly to the end of v. 17, reading "a reproach to the adversaries" while lacking MT's "zeal" (v. 17) and the recompense to the coastlands (v. 18b).
notes.59:20: LXX reads "for the sake of Zion" (heneken Seion), differing from MT "to Zion" and Paul's citation "out of Zion" in Romans 11:26.
notes.60:1: LXX doubles the passive/middle imperative "Be illuminated, be illuminated" and explicitly names Jerusalem, where MT reads "Arise, shine."
notes.60:6: Greek reads Gaipha (representing the initial Hebrew consonant ayin with gamma) and Saba, transliterating Ephah and Sheba.
notes.60:9: Greek "and the holy name of the Lord" lacks a preposition (corresponding to Heb. lesem, "for the name"), and "because the Holy One of Israel is glorious" differs from MT "because He has glorified you."
notes.60:18: LXX reads Glymma ("Carving" or "carved work") for your gates, where MT reads "Praise" (tehillah).
notes.60:21: LXX "guarding the planting, the works of His hands" reads Heb. neser ("branch/shoot") as noser ("guarding") and shifts first-person "My planting, the work of My hands" to third-person "His hands" (cf. 61:3).
notes.61:1: LXX has "recovery of sight to the blind" (the form quoted in Luke 4:18-19) where MT reads "opening of the prison to those who are bound."
notes.61:3: LXX renders MT's "oaks of righteousness" as "generations of righteousness" and reads "to those who mourn" (dative) rather than "instead of mourning."
notes.61:7: LXX differs markedly from MT ("instead of your shame you will have a double portion"), reading "Thus they will inherit the land a second time."
notes.61:10: The opening clause ("and with gladness they will be glad in the Lord") continues the third-person plural description of 61:9 in LXX before shifting to the first-person speaker.
notes.61:11: Greek doubles the title as kyrios Kyrios ("the Lord, the Lord"), corresponding to Hebrew Adonai YHWH.
notes.62:1: LXX reads "My salvation" (spoken by the Lord) where MT has "her salvation."
notes.62:4: LXX renders Hebrew Hephzibah ("My delight is in her") as "My Delight" (lit. "My Will/Desire") and Beulah ("Married") as "Inhabited," linking the verse to the dwelling wordplay in 62:5.
notes.62:7: LXX differs from MT ("and give Him no rest until He establishes..."), reading "there is no one like you" and leaving an open conditional clause ("if He establishes," lit. "sets straight").
notes.62:8: Greek introduces the negative oath with the Hebraistic conditional idiom ei eti (lit. "if still/again"), meaning "I will certainly no longer."
notes.63:1: Greek "Bosor" is the standard LXX rendering of Bozrah; LXX reads "redness of garments," "with force," and "judgment of salvation" where MT has "crimsoned garments," "marching," and "mighty to save."
notes.63:3: LXX reads "full of a trampled [winepress]" (a feminine singular participle, καταπεπατημένης, agreeing with the winepress, ληνός, of 63:2) where MT has "I have trodden the winepress alone."
notes.63:9: LXX reads "Not an envoy nor an angel [or 'messenger'], but He Himself saved them" where MT has "In all their affliction He was afflicted, and the angel of His presence saved them."
notes.63:14: Greek πνεῦμα παρὰ Κυρίου is anarthrous and can be rendered either "the Spirit ... from the Lord" or "a spirit from the Lord."
notes.63:18: LXX reads "so that we may inherit a little [or 'for a little while'] of Your holy mountain" and omits the second half of the verse found in MT.
notes.63:19: In LXX, the second half of 63:19 corresponds to MT 64:1a and breaks mid-sentence ("and they will melt") before continuing into 64:1.
notes.64:1: In the Septuagint versification, 64:1 begins mid-sentence as a direct continuation of the clause at the end of 63:19.
notes.64:4: The Greek verb synantēsetai is third-person singular ('He will meet,' or potentially 'it will meet,' referring to mercy or Your works), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads second-person 'You meet.'
notes.64:5: Greek apokathēmenēs literally means 'of a woman sitting apart,' the standard Septuagint term for a menstruating woman in ceremonial separation (cf. Leviticus 15).
notes.64:8: Greek en kairō ('in time') differs from 'forever' in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, likely reflecting a reading of the Hebrew as 'at a time' rather than 'forever.'
notes.64:9: The phrase 'for a curse' (eis kataran) at the end of 64:9 has no counterpart in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and continues directly into the opening clause of 64:10.
notes.65:8: The Septuagint reads singular 'him who serves Me' (tou douleuontos moi) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has plural 'My servants.'
notes.65:10: Greek en tō drymō ('in the forest') translates the Hebrew place name 'Sharon' as a common noun.
notes.65:11: Greek 'the demon' (tō daimoniō) and 'Fortune' (tē tychē) render the deity names Gad and Meni in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.65:15: Greek eis plēsmonēn ('for satiety' or 'to surfeit') reflects Hebrew śābʿâ ('satiety') where the Masoretic Text reads šəbûʿâ ('oath/curse').
notes.65:22: The Septuagint reads 'the tree of life' (tou xylou tēs zōēs), adding 'of life' compared to the Hebrew Masoretic Text's 'a tree.'
notes.66:3: The Septuagint introduces the verse with 'the lawless one' (ho anomos) and reads 'like one who kills a dog,' whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text begins 'He who slaughters an ox is like one who strikes down a man.'
notes.66:5: The Greek renders this as an imperative ('Say, our brothers, to those who hate you...') followed by a purpose clause, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reports the enemies' speech ('Your brothers who hate you... say, "May the Lord be glorified"').
notes.66:9: The Septuagint reads 'I gave this expectation, and you did not remember Me,' differing markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ('Shall I bring to the point of birth and not cause to bring forth?').
notes.66:19: The Septuagint lists Put (Phoud), Meshech (Mosoch), and Greece (Hellas) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has 'Pul,' 'who draw the bow,' and 'Javan.'
notes.66:20: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'on dromedaries' and 'in a clean vessel,' the Septuagint reads 'in covered wagons of mules with sunshades' and 'to Me with psalms.'
